The laser harp is an electrophonic electronic instrument and also a laser light display. It replaces the strings of a traditional harp with several laser beams, and the player produces sound by interrupting the beams with the hands, so visually it resembles a harp. Its popularity is owed to the French electronic music artist Jean-Michel Jarre, who has used it in almost all his concerts since 1981. Concerts by the British singer-songwriter Little Boots have used a similar version, and the Japanese electronic music composer Hirasawa Susumu is regarded as the best-known player of the instrument in Asia.
雷射豎琴的主要結構由金屬框架構成，內部搭載高功率雷射發射裝置（通常採用紅色或綠色: The laser harp's main structure is a metal frame carrying high-power laser transmitters, usually red or green laser diodes. The sound is produced by precision electronic circuitry and a digital signal processor. The instrument has no traditional wooden soundbox or strings, and uses optical sensors to detect interruption of the beams. The casing is often made of modern composite materials or aluminium alloy, reinforcing the technological look and durability.
雷射豎琴的起源與專利申請有關：法國作曲家Bernard Szajner於1981: The origin of the laser harp is bound up with patents: the French composer Bernard Szajner applied in 1981 and was granted a patent in 1982; the Australian inventor Geoffrey Rose claims to have filed a provisional patent in Britain in 1975–76, and his device may have been demonstrated as early as 1976. Jean-Michel Jarre then promoted it in concerts from 1981, making it a well-known feature. In 2005 a free multicolour laser harp project was shared on a laser discussion board and shown at a gathering in Germany.
雷射豎琴的音色明亮、清晰而富有現代感，帶有電子合成音的典型特徵。其音質具有冷冽的: The laser harp's timbre is bright, clear and modern, with the typical character of electronic synthesis. Its quality has a cold metallic ring yet does not lose the elegance of a harp's tone. Its range is wide, spanning several octaves; the bass is deep and powerful, the treble crisp and exciting. The sound is not made through a traditional soundbox but amplified and output directly by electronic circuitry, so it lacks the warmth of a wooden instrument. Against the soft warmth of the traditional harp the laser harp is more penetrating; against an electronic synthesiser it keeps the layered timbre of plucked harp. Its distinctive sound combines the aesthetics of the classical instrument and modern electronic music, creating a listening experience full of technology that does not lose its musicality.
